newsitem.title: THAILAND: Tough Thai measures fail to allay fears for economy.
newsitem.headline: Tough Thai measures fail to allay fears for economy.

text.p: Tough measures unleashed on Tuesday to revive Thailand's economy in the midst of its worst turmoil in decades caught analysts unprepared but failed to dispel concerns for the future.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya announced Thailand would seek $12-$15 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other governments, partly to replenish its depleted foreign reserves.
The loans would only be obtained after Thailand brought its economy under control and met a series of targets recommended by the IMF, however.

One of those was a drastic revamp of the finance sector. Tough measures introduced on Tuesday included suspending 42 finance firms to help ease the burden on a government that has been compelled to lend hundreds of billions of baht to cash-strapped companies.
Many analysts said they were surprised by the Bank of Thailand's decision to suspend the companies, bringing the number of finance firms which have been told to stop operations since late June to 58.
The firms accounted for nearly two thirds of companies in the 91-member non-bank finance sector.
The move ignited hectic selling on the stock market and overshadowed the overall IMF package, while the baht sagged.

"The expanded suspension is too drastic and unwarranted with its unknown impacts. There are other softer alternatives that it could have taken. The suspension was based on some unclear criteria," said Kitti Limsakul, economist at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University.
Kitti and other analysts pointed out that many of the firms suspended on Tuesday had been in the process of merging with other stronger local companies or courting foreign partners.

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi told a news conference the suspended firms, with combined public deposits of 300-400 billion baht ($9.7-12.9 billion), would stop lending and most other business for at least three months.
He said auditors would review the financial positions of the firms in two months time. In the meantime they would need to come up with "rehabilitation" plans.
Vuth Puthamon, an analyst at Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand Plc, one of the firms suspended on Tuesday, said: "I think I'd better starting looking for a new job."

One of the issues generating active domestic debate was the increase of the value added tax (VAT) to 10 percent from seven, effective August 16. Government officials said the hike would produce over 70 billion baht tax revenue annually.
"The government is scratching at the wrong spot. It's unfortunate that it resorted to letting the majority of Thais suffer instead of cutting more budgets," Kitti said.
Finance ministry officials said the VAT hike was among measures recommended by the IMF.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said his six-party coalition government was prepared to slash up to 100 billion baht from its 1997/1998 (October-September) fiscal budget. He did not specify which government agencies would bear the brunt of budget cuts.
He said the IMF projected Thailand's economy would recover by 1999 due to its strong basic fundamentals.

Other measures announced by the government and recommended by the IMF included a cap on inflation and the current account deficit and a minimum level of gross domestic product growth and foreign reserves.

But one university lecturer said he was sceptical that Thailand could keep its inflation and current account deficit under control after the baht lost about 20 percent of its value since the de facto devaluation of the Thai currency on July 2. He said the higher VAT would add more upward price pressure.

An analyst at a finance firm further predicted that inflation would surge to about 15 percent in 1998 from a projected 6.1 percent this year despite Thanong's target to curb price increases to 8-9 percent.
